You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14-26, which are based on Reading Passage 2
on pages 6 and 7.
The Coastal Archaeology of Britain
Recognition of the wealth of Britain's coastal archaeology has been one of the most
important developments in British archaeology in recent years. Some elements of this
enormous resource have long been known. The so-called ‘submerged forests’ off the
coasts of Britain attracted the interest of antiquarians in the eighteenth century, but
serious and systematic attention has been given to the archaeological potential of the
coast only since the early 1980s.
At this time, scientific research into climate change and its environmental impact
spilled over into a much broader public debate as understanding of the issues grew. The
prospect of rising sea levels over the next century and their impact on current coastal
environments have been a particular focus for concern. At the same time, archaeologists
were beginning to recognise the increasingly damaging effect of human activity.
The dominant process affecting the physical form of Britain in the post-glacial period
has been the rise in sea level relative to the land, as the glaciers have melted and the
landmass readjusted. The loss of huge areas of land now under the North Sea and the
English Channel, especially the land bridge between England and France, must have
been an immensely significant factor in the lives of our prehistoric ancestors. Yet the
way in which they adjusted to these changes has hardly been discussed, partly because
little is known about the constant reconfiguration of the coastline.
So great has been the rise in sea level and the consequent regression of the coast that
much of the archaeological evidence now exposed in the coastal zone is derived from
what was originally terrestrial occupation, and can tell us little about past adaptations
to the sea. Nevertheless, its physical environment means that preservation is often
excellent, for example in the case of the Neolithic structure excavated at The Stumble in
Essex.
Where evidence does relate to past human exploitation of the sea, it is both diverse and
little understood. We are not yet in a position to make even preliminary estimates
concerning the extent to which the sea and the coast affected human life in the past,
what percentage of the population at any time lived within reach of the sea, or whether
human settlements in coastal environments were distinct from those inland.

The most striking evidence for use of the sea is in the form of boats, yet we still have
much to learn about their production and use. Most of the known wrecks around the
British coast are post-medieval and offer an unparalleled opportunity for research which
has as yet been little used. The prehistoric sewn-plank boats, such as those from the
Humber estuary and Dover, all seem to belong to the second millennium BC. After this
there is a gap in the record of a millennium, which cannot yet be explained, before boats
reappear, but built using a very different technology. Boats were some of the most
complex artefacts produced by pre-modern societies, and further research on their
production and use could make an important contribution to our understanding of past
attitudes to technology and technological change.
Boats need landing places, yet here again our knowledge is very patchy. In later
periods, many ports and harbours, as well as smaller facilities such as quays, wharves
and jetties, were built. Yet despite a growth of interest in the waterfront archaeology of
some of our more important Roman and medieval towns, very little attention has been
paid to these smaller landing places. Redevelopment of harbour sites and other natural
pressures along the coast are subjecting them to unprecedented threats, yet few surveys
of such sites have been undertaken.
One of the most important revelations of recent research has been the extent of
industrial activity along the coast. Fishing and salt production are among the better
documented activities, but even here our knowledge is patchy. A recent survey has
revealed the extent of past investment in facilities for procuring fish and shellfish.
Elaborate wooden fish weirs, often of considerable extent and responsive to aerial
photography in shallow water, have been identified in areas such as Essex and the
Severn estuary. The production of salt, especially in the late Iron Age and early Roman
periods, has been recognised for some time, but the reasons for the disappearance of that
industry are much less well understood. Mineral resources such as sand, gravel, stone,
coal, ironstone and alum were also exploited, but although the remains of these
industries are sometimes extensive and striking, they are poorly documented. However,
one of the biggest gaps in our knowledge is the nature of the human settlements
associated with the exploitation of the sea.
Some appreciation of the variety and importance of coastal archaeological remains can
thus be gained from recent work. However, the difficulty of managing that resource is
also becoming clear. The problem arises not only from the scale of the archaeological
remains themselves, but also from natural and human threats to the resource, and the
complexity of the web of organisations with authority over it. Human threats include
the redevelopment of historic towns and old dockland areas, and the expanding leisure
and tourism industries. The larger size of ferries has also resulted in increased damage
to fragile deposits in the intertidal zone. The most significant natural threat is the
predicted rise in sea level over the next century, especially in the south and east of
England.

A public interest in our prehistoric ancestors
B the discovery of underwater forests
c awareness of impending coastal changes
D the increasing economic importance of the coast

B has been exposed by falling water levels.
Cc contrasts with evidence from inland sites.
D is in poor physical condition.

A Post-medieval wrecks have been extensively studied.
B There is a period of a thousand years for which no evidence exists.
c Boat building was confined to certain parts of the coast.

A human settlements.
B salt production.
c mine workings.
D the fishing industry.
